planting.note: Set divisions out just after snowmelt in spring into gritty, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil, mimicking the plant's natural subalpine snowmelt-zone awakening.

directions: Primula cuneifolia forms a tight rosette of small, wedge-shaped (spoon-like), toothed leaves, giving the species its name, native to alpine and subalpine meadows, snowmelt seeps, and rocky slopes of Hokkaido, Sakhalin, Kamchatka, and the Aleutians. In late spring to early summer it sends up short umbels of pink to purple-violet flowers with a small yellow eye held just above the foliage. It demands cool summers, constant moisture at the root, and sharp drainage, conditions best replicated in a scree bed, alpine trough, or alpine house rather than a conventional border, and it resents hot, humid, or dry conditions. Propagate by careful division of established clumps in spring or by fresh seed, since plants are slow from older seed and short-lived without division.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines
